seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 37 HTS Chapter 86 lines: locomotives, passenger and freight railcars, rail parts (wheels, axles, brakes, couplers), track fixtures, signaling equipment and shipping containers (8609). 23 lines pay 25% Section 232 from every country; China adds 25%; couplers carry AD/CVD.

overview.intro:
Chapter 86 covers railway and tramway equipment: electric, battery and diesel locomotives (8601–8602), self-propelled rail cars (8603), track maintenance vehicles (8604), passenger coaches (8605), freight cars (8606), parts such as trucks, wheels, axles, brakes and couplers (8607), track fixtures and mechanical signaling equipment (8608), and shipping and intermodal containers (8609). **9 of the 37 lines are Free** under the general rate; the rest pay 0.4% to 14% (railcars and coaches 14%), and USMCA and most other FTAs make them Free.

What decides the cost is **Section 232**. **23 lines pay +25% of the full customs value** (heading 9903.82.09, U.S. note 16(c)(vii)) from every country, on top of any FTA or USMCA rate: all locomotives, self-propelled cars, service vehicles and passenger coaches, tank cars, most parts (wheels, axles, couplers, locomotive parts) and containers. Lower rates: **15%** for UK goods of at least 95% UK-melted steel and **10%** for goods whose steel is at least 85% U.S.-melted. The other **14 lines** (hopper, box, gondola and flat cars, bolsters and side frames, freight-car brakes and some other parts, and 8608 track and signaling equipment) are outside Section 232 and pay the 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5%, or 10% to 12.5% in place of the base rate for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland) unless they qualify for USMCA.

China pays another **25%** under Section 301 on almost every line (containers excepted), and freight rail couplers from China and Mexico carry **antidumping and countervailing duties** that also reach couplers fitted to imported railcars; they are not part of this table or the tariff calculator (see Tariff updates).

productGroups.label: Electric & battery locomotives
productGroups.blurb: Rail locomotives powered from an external source of electricity (8601.10) or by batteries (8601.20): 2 lines, both Free. Both have been Section 232 derivative steel articles since August 18, 2025 (50% on the steel content), and since April 6, 2026 pay 25% of the full value (9903.82.09).

productGroups.label: Diesel-electric & other locomotives
productGroups.blurb: Diesel-electric locomotives (8602.10) and other locomotives and tenders (8602.90): 2 lines, both Free, both +25% Section 232. Duty-free locomotives used to be released without a formal entry; with Section 232 duty owed they now need one.

productGroups.label: Self-propelled rail cars (EMU, DMU, light rail)
productGroups.blurb: Self-propelled railway or tramway coaches, vans and trucks, electric (8603.10) or other (8603.90): 2 lines at 5% (Free under USMCA and most FTAs), +25% Section 232 on top of any FTA rate.

productGroups.label: Track maintenance & service vehicles
productGroups.blurb: Railway maintenance or service vehicles such as ballast tampers, track inspection vehicles, workshops and rail cranes: 1 line at 2.9%, +25% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Passenger coaches (not self-propelled)
productGroups.blurb: Passenger coaches, luggage vans, post office and other special-purpose coaches without their own power: 1 line at 14% (Free under USMCA and most FTAs), +25% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Freight cars (tank, hopper, box, gondola, flat)
productGroups.blurb: Railway freight cars, not self-propelled: tank cars (8606.10), self-discharging hoppers (8606.30), covered box cars (8606.91), open gondolas (8606.92) and flatcars and other cars (8606.99): 6 lines at 14%, Free under USMCA. Only tank cars are on the Section 232 list (+25%); the other five pay the 2026 Section 301 duty for most countries unless an FTA applies.

productGroups.label: Railcar & locomotive parts (trucks, wheels, axles, brakes, couplers)
productGroups.blurb: Parts of locomotives and rolling stock: truck assemblies (bogies), axles and wheels, bolsters and side frames, air and other brakes, couplers, buffers and other parts: 21 lines, Free to 3.9%. 14 lines pay +25% Section 232; truck assemblies of 8607.12, bolsters and side frames, the brake lines for freight and passenger cars of 8607.21.10 and 8607.29, and 8607.99.10 parts are outside it. Freight rail couplers carry AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Track fixtures & mechanical signaling
productGroups.blurb: Railway or tramway track fixtures and fittings, assembled track, turntables, buffers and mechanical (including electro-mechanical) signaling, safety and traffic control equipment for railways, roads, waterways, parking, ports and airfields, and parts: 1 line at 3.8%. Not on the Section 232 lists; electrical signaling is heading 8530 and steel track material 7302.

productGroups.label: Shipping & intermodal containers
productGroups.blurb: Containers, including tank containers, specially designed for carriage by one or more modes of transport (ISO shipping containers, 53-foot domestic containers): 1 line, Free. +25% Section 232 since April 6, 2026 (50% on the steel content from August 18, 2025). Containers arriving in use in international traffic are released without entry or duty.

workedExamples.title: Open-top hopper or gondola cars from Mexico
workedExamples.body: Open freight cars carry a **14%** base rate, but they are **Free** under USMCA and not on the Section 232 lists, so a USMCA-qualifying car pays **nothing**. Without a USMCA claim it pays 14% plus the **10%** 2026 Section 301 duty on Mexico (9903.05.55): **24%**. A duty-free freight car can be released without a formal entry under a CBP bond (19 CFR 141.4(b)(4)). Couplers on the car that were cast in China or Mexico are still subject to the coupler AD/CVD orders.

workedExamples.title: Railway tank cars from Mexico
workedExamples.body: Tank cars are the one freight car on the Section 232 list: **+25%** of the full value (9903.82.09) even with USMCA (note 16(b)), so a USMCA tank car pays **25%** and a non-qualifying one **39%** (14% + 25%). A $150,000 car owes $37,500. An antidumping and countervailing duty petition on Mexican tank cars was filed on September 30, 2026.

workedExamples.title: Shipping containers from China
workedExamples.body: Containers are **Free** at base and on none of the China Section 301 lists, but they are Section 232 derivatives: **+25%** (9903.82.09), so **25%** in total; the 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not apply to Section 232 goods. USTR proposed 20% to 100% on Chinese containers in April 2025 but dropped it in October 2025. A container that arrives in use in international traffic is released without entry or duty (19 CFR 10.41a).

workedExamples.title: Assembled freight rail couplers from China
workedExamples.body: Base rate **3.6%**, plus **+25%** Section 232 (9903.82.09) and **+25%** Section 301 (List 2, 9903.88.02): **53.6%**. On top of that come the antidumping cash deposit (139.49%) and the countervailing duty (265.99%), so Chinese couplers cost more than four times their value in duty.

workedExamples.title: Wheel sets and axles from Japan
workedExamples.body: Other parts of axles and wheels pay **2.6%**, Free under the U.S.-Japan Trade Agreement (JP), but **+25%** Section 232 applies on top: **25%**. If at least 85% of the steel was melted and poured in the United States, the importer can enter them under **9903.82.06 at +10%**.

workedExamples.title: Mechanical signaling equipment from Germany
workedExamples.body: Heading 8608 is not on the Section 232 lists. The EU rate under the 2026 Section 301 action is **10% in place of** the 3.8% base rate (9903.05.39): **10%**. Electrical signaling equipment is heading 8530, not Chapter 86.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) railway or tramway sleepers (cross-ties) of wood or of concrete, or concrete guide-track sections for hovertrains (heading 4406 or 6810); (b) railway or tramway track construction material of iron or steel of heading 7302; or (c) electrical signaling, safety or traffic control equipment of heading 8530.

**Note 2.** Heading 8607 applies, inter alia, to: (a) axles, wheels, wheel sets (running gear), metal tires, hoops and hubs and other parts of wheels; (b) frames, underframes, truck assemblies; (c) axle boxes; brake gear; (d) buffers for rolling-stock; hooks and other coupling gear and corridor connections; (e) coachwork.

**Note 3.** Subject to note 1, heading 8608 applies, inter alia, to: (a) assembled track, turntables, platform buffers, loading gauges; (b) semaphores, mechanical signal discs, level crossing control gear, signal and point controls, and other mechanical (including electro-mechanical) signaling, safety or traffic control equipment, whether or not fitted for electric lighting, for railways, tramways, roads, inland waterways, parking facilities, port installations or airfields.

**Section XVII notes (summary).** Parts of general use of base metal, machines of 8401–8479, electrical equipment of chapter 85 and instruments of chapter 90 are not "parts" of rail vehicles; vehicles built to run on both road and rail are classified in chapter 87; and hovertrain track fixtures and signaling are classified with railway track fixtures and signaling.
notes.additionalUsNotes: **1.** Railway locomotives (headings 8601 and 8602) and railway freight cars (heading 8606) on which no duty is owed are not subject to the entry or release requirements of sections 448 and 484 of the Tariff Act of 1930. The Secretary of the Treasury may by regulation establish reporting requirements, including a bond (see 19 CFR 141.4(b)(4) and (d)).

seo.title: Railcar, Locomotive & Container Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Section 232 25%, China 301, Coupler AD/CVD (HTS Ch. 86) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every U.S. tariff change on HTS Chapter 86 rail equipment and containers since 2025, with Federal Register citations: Section 232 on locomotives, railcars, parts and containers (August 2025, full value from April 6, 2026), the 2026 Section 301 duties, the end of IEEPA, the dropped container tariff, and AD/CVD on freight rail couplers and tank cars.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) with the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026) and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 86 today. No base rate changed; three statistical lines now split freight rail couplers (8607.30.10) into assembled couplers, coupler parts and other.

The extra duties changed completely. Chapter 86 had no Section 232 duty until **August 18, 2025**, when Commerce's first inclusions round added 22 locomotive, railcar, parts and container provisions as derivative steel articles at 50% of their steel content. Proclamation 11021 rebuilt the program on **April 6, 2026**: **25% of the full customs value**, with tank cars (8606.10) added. The IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026**, the Section 122 surcharge expired on **July 23, 2026**, and the 2026 Section 301 duties leave Section 232 goods alone, so they reach only the 14 lines outside Section 232. China's 2018 Section 301 duties stack on top.

Antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover freight rail couplers from China and Mexico (also when fitted to railcars), investigations on Czech and Indian couplers are at the final stage, and a petition on Mexican tank cars was filed in September 2026. They are company-specific and **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 86 from any country: Section 232 derivative steel articles (note 16), China Section 301 (note 20, Lists 1–3), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and Brazil (notes 50, 52), Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. No Canada Section 338 list (note 51), China note 31 heading or Section 232 vehicle-parts heading reaches Chapter 86. The AD/CVD orders and investigations on Chapter 86 products are summarized for reference; the calculator does not model them. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.country: All countries (Canada, Mexico, EU, Japan, Korea and Brazil included); Russia under 9903.82.16, also 25%
inEffect.measure: Section 232 derivative steel articles, on the full customs value
inEffect.before: None until August 18, 2025; then +50% on the steel content (9903.81.91) for 22 provisions; tank cars none
inEffect.exemption: Covers 23 lines on note 16(c)(vii): locomotives (8601, 8602), self-propelled cars (8603), service vehicles (8604), passenger coaches (8605), tank cars (8606.10), truck assemblies for self-propelled vehicles (8607.11), axles, wheels and their parts (8607.19.03–.15, .90), air brakes other than for 8605/8606 cars (8607.21.50), couplers and buffers (8607.30), locomotive parts (8607.91), other parts (8607.99.50) and containers (8609). Not covered: 8606.30–8606.99, 8607.12, 8607.19.30, 8607.21.10, 8607.29, 8607.99.10 and 8608. No country exemptions; note 16(b) collects it on top of any FTA or USMCA rate. Goods under 9903.82.09 do not pay the 2026 Section 301 or Brazil duties (notes 52(f)(1), 50(a)(vi)(1)).

changes.title: No Chapter 86 base-rate changes
changes.detail: 34 of 37 Chapter 86 lines carry the same rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Freight rail couplers for heading 8605 and 8606 cars (8607.30.10) are now split into assembled couplers (8607.30.10.10), coupler parts (8607.30.10.50) and other (8607.30.10.90), all at the unchanged 3.6%.

changes.title: AD/CVD petition on railway tank cars from Mexico
changes.detail: UTLX Manufacturing petitioned on September 30, 2026 for antidumping and countervailing duties on railway tank cars and parts from Mexico (8606.10). The ITC instituted its investigations; its preliminary vote is due by November 16, 2026, and Commerce sets any cash deposits after its own preliminary determinations.

changes.title: Final AD/CVD determinations on couplers from the Czech Republic and India
changes.detail: Commerce made final affirmative determinations on freight rail couplers and parts (8607.30.10): Czech dumping margin 73.74%; Indian dumping margins 2.32%–71.01% (all others 5.24%) and subsidy rates 9.71%–75% (all others 9.71%). Orders follow only if the ITC's final injury vote, due within 45 days, is affirmative.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: only lines outside Section 232 pay
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% duties on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. They do not apply to Section 232 goods (note 52(f)(1)), so in Chapter 86 they reach only the 14 lines outside Section 232: hopper, box, gondola and flat cars, some truck and brake parts and 8608 signaling equipment. USMCA goods are exempt; for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland the rate replaces the base rate when it is higher.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It did not apply to Section 232 goods or USMCA goods (Proclamation 11012), so in Chapter 86 it had charged the non-USMCA lines outside Section 232.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil: Section 232 goods exempt
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Section 232 goods are excluded (note 50(a)(vi)(1)), so it reaches only the 14 lines outside Section 232.

changes.title: Proclamation 11032: 85% U.S.-melted test
changes.detail: From June 8, 2026, a derivative article qualifies for the 10% rate (9903.82.06) when at least 85% of its steel content by weight was melted and poured in the United States (before, all of it). Chapter 86 rates (25%) did not change.

changes.title: Mexico coupler AD rate cut to 6.50% in first review
changes.detail: Commerce's first administrative review of the antidumping order on freight rail couplers from Mexico set a 6.50% margin for Amsted Rail / ASF-K de Mexico (period May 2023 to October 2024); that is now the company's cash deposit rate. Other Mexican producers stay at 48.10%.

changes.title: Section 232 rebuilt on full value: 25% for Chapter 86 (Proclamation 11021)
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 replaced the earlier headings with 9903.82.02–9903.82.26, charged on the full customs value regardless of metal content. The 22 Chapter 86 derivative lines moved to the 25% list (9903.82.09), and railway tank cars (8606.10) were added to it. New lower rates: UK 15% with ≥95% UK-melted steel, 10% for goods of U.S.-melted steel. Manufacturing drawback is allowed for these 25% list goods from trade-agreement partners; goods admitted to a foreign-trade zone must take privileged foreign status; the inclusions process ended.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. It did not apply to Section 232 goods or to USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026. Section 232 and Section 301 duties are not IEEPA duties and continued. For Chapter 86 the IEEPA duties had applied to the non-steel content of the derivative lines and to all other lines.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29). Note 29 has no Section 232 carve-out, so it will add to the 25% on Nicaraguan locomotives, parts and containers. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: ITC reconsiders its China coupler injury finding on court remand
changes.detail: The Court of International Trade sent the ITC's 2023 injury determination on Chinese freight rail couplers back for reconsideration (Wabtec v. United States, Slip Op. 25-134). The China AD and CVD orders stay in force while the remand runs.

changes.title: Maritime Section 301 actions suspended for a year
changes.detail: After the November 1, 2025 U.S.-China deal, USTR suspended all actions in the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding Section 301 investigation from November 10, 2025 through November 9, 2026, including the 100% duty on Chinese intermodal chassis (8716, chapter 87). No Chapter 86 product was covered.

changes.title: USTR decides not to tariff Chinese shipping containers
changes.detail: In its final maritime Section 301 action, USTR imposed duties on ship-to-shore cranes and intermodal chassis but decided not to impose the proposed duties on intermodal shipping containers (8609), citing the impact on domestic intermodal carriers.

changes.title: Section 232 reaches Chapter 86: locomotives, railcars, parts and containers
changes.detail: Commerce's first inclusions round added 22 Chapter 86 provisions as derivative steel articles: 8601, 8602, 8603, 8604, 8605, 8607.11, 8607.19 (axles, wheels and parts), 8607.21.50, 8607.30 couplers, 8607.91, 8607.99.50 and 8609 containers. The 50% duty applied to the value of the steel content; the non-steel content kept paying the reciprocal and other IEEPA duties.

changes.title: New coupler investigations on the Czech Republic and India
changes.detail: Commerce opened antidumping investigations on freight rail couplers and parts from the Czech Republic and India and a countervailing duty investigation on India.

changes.title: USTR proposes tariffs on Chinese containers
changes.detail: In the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding Section 301 action, USTR proposed duties of 20% to 100% on containers of China (8609.00.00) and on intermodal chassis and parts. The container duty was dropped in October 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariffs reach Chapter 86
changes.detail: Executive Order 14257 set a 10% reciprocal tariff on most countries from April 5, 2025, raised to country rates from August 7, 2025 (Executive Order 14326). Chapter 86 had no Section 232 duty then, so it paid them in full; Canadian and Mexican goods paid the separate IEEPA duties instead. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: IEEPA duties on Canada, Mexico and China
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025, with USMCA goods exempt from March 7, 2025, and +10% (then +20%) on goods of China. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: AD order on freight rail couplers from Mexico
changes.detail: Commerce issued an antidumping order on freight rail couplers and parts from Mexico at 48.10%. Like the China order, it covers couplers fitted to railcars, by the country where the coupler parts were cast.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on freight rail couplers from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping (China-wide 169.90%, cash deposit 139.49%) and countervailing duty (265.99%) orders on freight rail couplers, knuckles and coupler bodies from China, including those fitted to railcars of 8606 entered from third countries.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 raised to 25% (other locomotives)
changes.detail: List 3 (9903.88.03), which in Chapter 86 covers other locomotives and tenders (8602.90), went from 10% (September 24, 2018) to 25%.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 2: railcars, couplers and more
changes.detail: List 2 (9903.88.02, 25%) took effect on August 23, 2018, covering battery and diesel-electric locomotives, passenger coaches, all freight cars, some truck and axle parts and couplers.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 1: electric locomotives, self-propelled cars, most parts
changes.detail: List 1 (9903.88.01, 25%) took effect on July 6, 2018, covering electric locomotives, self-propelled cars, service vehicles, most wheels, axles, brakes and other parts, and 8608 signaling equipment.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 86 goods were **$1.83B in 2025**, down 28.4% from $2.55B in 2024 and well below the $3.25B peak of 2022. The five largest suppliers were China ($387M), Mexico ($320M), Canada ($233M), Japan ($165M), Germany ($105M). Parts of locomotives and rolling stock (8607) were the largest group at $1.08B, followed by containers (8609) at $554M; freight cars (8606) fell to $13M from $286M in 2024.

China's shipments, mostly containers ($220M) and parts ($159M), fell from $728M to $387M; Canada's more than halved to $233M, while Mexico held at $320M. 2025 is the year Section 232 reached the chapter: from August 18 most Chapter 86 goods paid 50% on their steel content, and since April 6, 2026 they pay 25% of their full value from every country.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For most of Chapter 86 the answer is the same everywhere: **25%** plus the base rate on the 23 Section 232 lines, because Section 232 has no country exemptions and is collected on top of FTA and USMCA rates. China pays **25% more** under Section 301 on almost every line, UK goods of UK-melted steel pay 15% (the cells show the default 25%), and goods of U.S.-melted steel pay 10%.

The 14 lines outside Section 232 (most freight cars, bolsters, side frames, some brake parts and 8608 signaling equipment) are where countries differ: Free for USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico, the base rate plus 10% or 12.5% for most of the 60 Section 301 economies, 10% or 12.5% in place of the base rate for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, and more for China and Brazil. The table does **not** include antidumping or countervailing duties (see Tariff updates).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 86: Railway Locomotives, Rolling Stock, Track Fixtures & Containers — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Locomotives, Railcars & Containers: Entry Rules, FRA Content Limits, Section 232 & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 86) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 86 line: Section 232 headings and melt-and-pour reporting, bond release of duty-free locomotives and freight cars, international-traffic admission of rail equipment and containers, FRA's freight car content limits, coupler AD/CVD scope, plus the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, U.S.-melted steel, drawback, repairs abroad and FTZs.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Rail equipment has its own entry rules. Locomotives and freight cars **on which no duty is owed** can be released without a formal entry under a CBP bond (Chapter 86 additional U.S. note 1; 19 CFR 141.4), but Section 232 now puts duty on locomotives and tank cars, so they need a regular entry. Foreign locomotives and railcars running through on a cross-border route, and containers arriving in use in international traffic, are admitted **without entry or duty** (19 CFR 123.12, 10.41a). Every Section 232 entry reports 9903.82.09 (or a lower-rate heading) and the **country where the steel was melted and poured**. New freight cars must also meet FRA's **content limits**: from December 19, 2025, no more than 20% of a car's content may come from a country of concern or a state-owned enterprise there.

The legal ways to pay less: **USMCA** for Canadian and Mexican cars and parts (it removes the base rate and the 2026 Section 301 duty, but not Section 232), steel that is **U.S.-melted** (10%) or **UK-melted** (15%), **drawback** on these 25% list goods from trade-agreement partners, the **Chapter 98** treatment for U.S. equipment returned or repaired abroad, **foreign-trade zones** for rail-car assembly, avoiding **Chinese origin**, and checking **AD/CVD scope** for couplers. Each rule and lever links to its regulation or proclamation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican railcars and parts
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 14% on railcars and coaches) on every line, plus the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty on the 14 lines outside Section 232 (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94)
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada or Mexico, in particular freight cars (8606), coaches (8605), self-propelled cars (8603) and dutiable parts
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, available to CBP on request; the railcar must meet the USMCA rule of origin for its heading.
levers.caveat: A USMCA claim does not reduce Section 232 (note 16(b)): tank cars, coaches and listed parts still pay 25%. A USMCA freight car outside Section 232 owes no duty and can be released under a bond without a formal entry.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 16(b) and 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Use U.S.-melted steel
levers.saves: 15 points of Section 232 (10% instead of 25%, heading 9903.82.06)
levers.appliesTo: The 23 Section 232 lines: locomotives, self-propelled cars, service vehicles, coaches, tank cars, wheels, axles, couplers, other listed parts and containers
levers.document: Mill certificates and supplier declarations showing the melt-and-pour country of the steel, enough to prove at least 85% (by weight) was melted and poured in the United States; reported in ACE.
levers.caveat: The 85% test applies from June 8, 2026 (before that, all of it). The base rate and China's Section 301 duty still apply.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(e), heading 9903.82.06

levers.title: Buy UK goods made of UK-melted steel
levers.saves: 10 points of Section 232 (15% instead of 25%, heading 9903.82.05)
levers.appliesTo: The 23 Section 232 lines, for products of the United Kingdom
levers.document: Mill test certificates and melt-and-pour reporting showing that at least 95% of the steel was melted and poured in the UK.
levers.caveat: Origin must be the UK and the 95% test must be met; otherwise 25%.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(d)

levers.title: Manufacturing drawback on Section 232 duty
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the Section 232 duty (and the ordinary duties) on imported equipment or parts used to make exported products
levers.appliesTo: The Section 232 lines (all on the Annex I-B 25% list) when they are products of the UK, EU, Japan, Korea, Mexico or Canada whose steel was entirely melted and poured in one of them; ordinary duties on all lines
levers.document: A manufacturing drawback claim to CBP under 19 U.S.C. 1313(a) or (b), with import, production and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Only manufacturing drawback qualifies (Proclamation 11021 clauses 13–14), and not for merchandise of a type under an AD/CVD order from any country, so freight rail couplers are out. AD/CVD are never refundable (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)).

levers.title: Keep containers and cross-border rail equipment in international traffic
levers.saves: The whole duty: equipment admitted as instruments of international traffic is not entered and pays no duty
levers.appliesTo: Containers (8609) arriving in use in international shipping, and foreign locomotives and railcars on a continuous cross-border run (8601–8606)
levers.document: No entry; the carrier reports the equipment. Containers must leave or be used under the conditions of 19 CFR 10.41a; foreign rail equipment may only do traffic incidental to its run (19 CFR 123.12).
levers.caveat: Containers or railcars kept for domestic use (for example 53-foot domestic containers or cars bought for U.S. service) must be formally entered and pay Section 232.

levers.title: U.S. equipment returned, or repaired abroad
levers.saves: The full duty on U.S.-built equipment returned unchanged (9801.00.10), or all but the duty on the repair value for cars repaired abroad (9802.00.40 / 9802.00.50; Free for USMCA repairs)
levers.appliesTo: U.S.-made locomotives, railcars and parts returned to the United States, and cars sent to Canada, Mexico or elsewhere for repair or rebuilding
levers.document: Proof of U.S. origin and export (9801.00.10), or the export record and the foreign repairer's invoice for the repair value (19 CFR 10.8).
levers.caveat: Note 16(b) keeps Chapter 98 treatment for Section 232 goods, so the Section 232 duty follows the Chapter 98 basis (for repairs, the value of the repair). A rebuild that creates a new article does not qualify.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(b)

levers.title: Assemble rolling stock in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: Duty deferral, and on components outside Section 232 the choice between the component rate and the rate on the finished car
levers.appliesTo: Rail-car and locomotive production in an FTZ with FTZ Board authority (for example, passenger rolling stock in Subzone 30G, Salt Lake City)
levers.document: An FTZ Board production notification and approval (15 CFR 400.14, 400.22), and zone admission records.
levers.caveat: Section 232 components must be admitted in privileged foreign status (Proclamation 11021 clause 12; 19 CFR 146.41), so they keep their 25% duty whatever the finished car's rate.

citations.label: FTZ Board notice for Stadler US (91 FR 15947)

levers.title: Avoid Chinese origin
levers.saves: 25% of the value: Chinese goods pay Section 301 on top of Section 232 (about 50% on most of the chapter), plus coupler AD/CVD
levers.appliesTo: Every Chapter 86 line except containers (8609), for goods of China
levers.document: Production records showing where the article was made; origin follows the last substantial transformation. For couplers, the AD/CVD orders follow the country where the coupler body or knuckle was cast.
levers.caveat: Third-country assembly does not change the Section 232 rate, and Chinese-cast couplers stay subject to the China AD/CVD orders even on cars finished elsewhere.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20

levers.title: Check coupler AD/CVD scope before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping or countervailing duty, when the coupler or producer is outside the order
levers.appliesTo: Freight rail couplers, knuckles and coupler bodies (8607.30.10), and railcars of 8606 fitted with them
levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides), where each coupler body and knuckle was cast, and the producer's cash-deposit rate; when unsure, request a scope ruling.
levers.caveat: Couplers on finished railcars are covered by casting origin. Locks, pins and other small parts imported alone are outside the orders.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling on borderline parts
levers.saves: Avoids paying the wrong rate: a part classified outside Chapter 86 (electrical signaling 8530, steel track material 7302, general-use parts) carries different duties
levers.appliesTo: Rail parts and track or signaling equipment (8607, 8608)
levers.document: A CBP binding ruling request with drawings and specifications; Section XVII note 2 and Chapter 86 notes 1–3 decide what counts as a rail part or track fixture.
levers.caveat: The ruling binds only for the goods described. Steel track material of 7302 pays 50% Section 232.

seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. tariffs on rail equipment: HTS Chapter 86 codes, railcar and tank car tariffs, locomotive and railway parts HS codes (8607), shipping container HS code 8609, the Section 232 steel derivative list, Mexico, Canada and China, and freight rail coupler duties.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most-searched questions about U.S. tariffs on railway equipment and containers (HTS Chapter 86), by product, by country and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the detail and the official sources.
keyTakeaways: 23 of the 37 Chapter 86 lines pay 25% Section 232 on their full customs value, from every country and on top of any FTA or USMCA rate: locomotives, self-propelled cars, service vehicles, passenger coaches, tank cars, wheels, axles, couplers, locomotive parts and containers. UK goods of UK-melted steel pay 15%, goods of U.S.-melted steel 10%.

The other 14 lines (hopper, box, gondola and flat cars, bolsters, side frames, some brake parts and 8608 signaling equipment) are outside Section 232: Free for USMCA goods, otherwise the base rate plus the 2026 Section 301 duty for most countries (10% or 12.5%).

China pays another 25% under Section 301 on almost every line except containers; freight rail couplers from China (AD 139.49% + CVD 265.99%) and Mexico carry AD/CVD, also when fitted to railcars. The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026 and the Section 122 surcharge July 23, 2026.
In 2025 the U.S. imported $1.83B of Chapter 86 goods (down 28.4% on 2024); China ($387M), Mexico ($320M) and Canada ($233M) were the largest suppliers.

faqs.question: What is HTS Chapter 86?
faqs.answer: Chapter 86 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule covers railway and tramway equipment: locomotives (8601–8602), self-propelled rail cars (8603), track maintenance vehicles (8604), passenger coaches (8605), freight cars (8606), parts of locomotives and rolling stock (8607), track fixtures and mechanical signaling equipment (8608) and containers for one or more modes of transport (8609). It has 37 ten-digit lines. Steel rails and track material are in chapter 73 (7302), electrical signaling in 8530, and road-rail vehicles in chapter 87.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on rail cars?
faqs.answer: It depends on the car. Passenger coaches (8605) and tank cars (8606.10) pay a 14% base rate (Free under USMCA and most FTAs) plus 25% Section 232 from every country; self-propelled cars pay 5% plus 25%. Hopper, box, gondola and flat cars (8606.30–8606.99) are outside Section 232: Free with USMCA, otherwise 14% plus the 2026 Section 301 duty (10% for Mexico and Canada). Chinese cars add 25% Section 301. Couplers on the car that were cast in China or Mexico carry AD/CVD.

faqs.question: Are railway tank cars subject to tariffs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tank cars (8606.10) were added to the Section 232 list on April 6, 2026: 25% of the full value from every country, on top of the 14% base rate (Free under USMCA). A USMCA-qualifying Mexican tank car pays 25%, a non-qualifying one 39%. On September 30, 2026 a U.S. maker petitioned for antidumping and countervailing duties on tank cars from Mexico; the ITC's preliminary vote is due by November 16, 2026.

faqs.question: What is HS code 8607 (railway parts)?
faqs.answer: Heading 8607 covers parts of railway locomotives and rolling stock: truck assemblies or bogies (8607.11–.12), axles, wheels and their parts and bolsters and side frames (8607.19), air and other brakes (8607.21, 8607.29), couplers and buffers (8607.30), locomotive parts (8607.91) and other parts (8607.99). Base rates run from Free to 3.9%. 14 of its 21 lines pay 25% Section 232; bolsters, side frames, 8607.12 trucks, brakes for freight and passenger cars (8607.21.10, 8607.29) and 8607.99.10 parts do not.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for shipping containers?
faqs.answer: Containers specially designed for carriage by one or more modes of transport, including ISO shipping containers, 53-foot domestic containers and tank containers, are 8609.00.00.00. The base rate is Free, but containers have paid Section 232 since August 18, 2025: now 25% of the full value from every country. A container that arrives in use in international traffic is released without entry or duty (19 CFR 10.41a); one imported for domestic use is entered and pays the 25%.

faqs.question: Is there an extra tariff on shipping containers from China?
searchedAs: how to import shipping container from china
faqs.answer: Only Section 232. Containers are on none of the China Section 301 lists, and the 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not apply to Section 232 goods, so a Chinese container pays 25%. USTR proposed 20% to 100% on Chinese containers in April 2025 but decided in October 2025 not to impose it. There is no AD/CVD order on containers: the ITC made negative final determinations on 53-foot domestic dry containers from China in 2015.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for locomotives?
faqs.answer: Electric and battery locomotives are 8601 and diesel-electric and other locomotives 8602. All four lines are Free at base, but they pay 25% Section 232 from every country (10% with U.S.-melted steel, 15% for UK goods of UK-melted steel), plus 25% Section 301 for China. Because duty is now owed, they no longer qualify for the bond release of duty-free locomotives; foreign locomotives on a cross-border run still enter without duty.

faqs.question: Which rail products are on the Section 232 steel derivatives list?
faqs.answer: U.S. note 16(c)(vii) to Chapter 99 lists 23 Chapter 86 lines at 25%: all locomotives, self-propelled cars, service vehicles and passenger coaches, tank cars, truck assemblies for self-propelled vehicles, axles, wheels and their parts, 8607.21.50 air brakes, couplers and buffers, locomotive parts, 8607.99.50 parts and containers. They were added on August 18, 2025 (tank cars on April 6, 2026). Since April 6, 2026 the duty is 25% of the full value, not just the steel content.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on railcars and rail parts from Mexico?
faqs.answer: With a USMCA claim, Mexican hopper, box, gondola and flat cars, bolsters, side frames and 8608 equipment are Free. The 23 Section 232 lines pay 25% with or without USMCA (tank cars, coaches, wheels, axles, couplers). Without USMCA, the base rate and, on the lines outside Section 232, 10% Section 301 are added. Mexican couplers pay AD (6.50% for Amsted / ASF-K, 48.10% others), and tank cars are under an AD/CVD petition. Mexico shipped $320M in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on rail equipment from Canada?
faqs.answer: Canadian goods pay 25% Section 232 on the 23 listed lines whether or not USMCA is claimed. Other freight cars, bolsters, side frames and 8608 equipment are Free with USMCA, otherwise base + 10% Section 301. No Chapter 86 line is on Canada's Section 338 lists. Rail equipment running through from Canada on a continuous route enters without duty. Canada shipped $233M in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on rail equipment from China?
faqs.answer: Most Chinese Chapter 86 goods pay about 50% plus the base rate: 25% Section 232 + 25% Section 301 (Lists 1, 2 or 3). Lines outside Section 232 pay the base rate + 25% + 12.5%; containers pay 25% only. Chinese freight rail couplers add AD 139.49% and CVD 265.99%. China shipped $387M in 2025.

faqs.question: Which freight rail couplers carry antidumping duties?
faqs.answer: Couplers, coupler bodies and knuckles meeting AAR standards from China (AD 139.49% + CVD 265.99%, orders of July 2023) and Mexico (AD, 6.50% for Amsted / ASF-K, 48.10% others) carry orders, including couplers fitted to railcars, by the country where they were cast. Commerce made final affirmative determinations on Czech and Indian couplers on September 24, 2026; orders follow if the ITC's final vote is affirmative.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import railcars, rail parts and shipping containers from?
searchedAs: where are most shipping containers made
faqs.answer: In 2025 the United States imported $1.83B of Chapter 86 goods, down 28% from 2024. The largest suppliers were China ($387M), Mexico ($320M), Canada ($233M), Japan ($165M), Germany ($105M). Parts (8607, $1.08B) and containers (8609, $554M) were the biggest groups.
